items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the thin, solid outer layer of the Earth, 5-10 km thick under oceans and up to about 70 km under mountains”.
items.answer: Crust
items.markingKey: Crust: the thin, solid outer layer of the Earth, 5-10 km thick under oceans and up to about 70 km under mountains. [1]

items.stem: Explain why volcanoes form at destructive plate boundaries.
items.answer: Denser oceanic plate subducts beneath the continental plate; as it sinks it melts (helped by water released) to form magma, which rises through cracks in the crust and erupts as volcanoes, e.g. the Andes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark subduction; 1 mark melting to magma; 1 mark magma rises/example [3]

items.stem: Explain why earthquakes but not volcanoes occur at conservative boundaries.
items.answer: Plates slide past each other and stick; pressure builds then is released suddenly as an earthquake; no crust is destroyed or created, so no magma rises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark plates stick and release; 1 mark no magma [2]

items.stem: Scientists measure that the Pacific plate sliding past the North American plate along the San Andreas Fault move past each other at about 4 cm per year. Calculate how far they move in 1 000 000 years  in kilometres.
items.answer: 40 km

items.stem: Scientists measure that the Nazca plate moving towards the South American plate move together at about 7 cm per year. (a) Calculate how far they move in 5 000 000 years  in kilometres. (b) Name the type of plate boundary.
items.answer: (a) 350 km (b) Destructive (or collision)

items.stem: How far do you agree that constructive plate boundaries are less hazardous to people than destructive plate boundaries? Use your own knowledge to support your answer. You may wish to consider: Iceland; earthquake size; types of eruption.
items.answer: Agree: Constructive boundaries usually produce gentle, effusive eruptions and smaller earthquakes. Many lie under oceans away from people. Disagree: Iceland’s Eyjafjallajökull (2010) ash cloud disrupted about 100 000 flights; Laki (1783) caused famine. Hazard also depends on how many people live nearby and how vulnerable they are. Judgement: Generally true – destructive boundaries produce the most violent eruptions, largest earthquakes and tsunamis – but impacts depend on population and preparedness.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: A student writes: “The Earth’s mantle is a liquid ocean of lava.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. The mantle is mostly solid rock that flows very slowly because it is so hot; only small parts melt to form magma.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Scientists measure that the Nazca plate moving towards the South American plate move together at about 7 cm per year. Calculate how far they move in 10 000 years  in kilometres.
items.answer: 0.7 km

items.stem: Scientists measure that the Indian plate moving north into the Eurasian plate move together at about 5 cm per year. (a) Name the type of plate boundary. (b) Describe one landform or hazard found at this type of boundary. (c) Explain what causes the plates to move.
items.answer: (a) Destructive (or collision) (b) Fold mountains (Himalayas, Andes), ocean trenches, explosive volcanoes and powerful earthquakes. (c) Convection currents in the mantle, together with ridge push and slab pull.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark landform/hazard; 1 mark example [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between the focus and the epicentre of an earthquake.
items.answer: The focus is the point underground where the rocks break and energy is released; the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it, where shaking is usually strongest.

items.answer: About 1 024 times

items.stem: Explain whether you agree that secondary effects of earthquakes are more serious than primary effects. Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.answer: Agree: The Tōhoku tsunami (2011) caused over 90% of deaths and the Fukushima nuclear accident. In Haiti (2010) a cholera outbreak later killed thousands; landslides cut off Nepali villages in 2015. Disagree: In many earthquakes, such as Nepal 2015 and Haiti 2010, most deaths came from buildings collapsing during the shaking. Primary effects destroy homes and infrastructure needed for recovery. Judgement: It depends on the event: for coastal subduction earthquakes secondary effects are often worse, for inland earthquakes primary effects usually dominate.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1 mark): one simple reason. Level 2 (2-3 marks): one explained reason for AND one against, with accurate detail.

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “a natural event, such as an earthquake or eruption, that threatens people and property”.

items.stem: Explain two reasons why people continue to live near active volcanoes.
items.answer: Fertile soils for farming; jobs in tourism and geothermal energy; minerals; family ties and a sense of home; eruptions are infrequent so people think the risk is low; poorer people may have nowhere else to go.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each explained reason [4]

items.stem: Explain how earthquake-resistant buildings reduce risk.
items.answer: Steel frames and cross-bracing let buildings sway without collapsing; base isolators absorb shaking; counterweights reduce movement in tall buildings; shatterproof glass and automatic gas shut-offs reduce injuries and fires.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each explained feature up to [3]

items.answer: (a) 10.5 (b) City E (10.5 compared with 6)

items.stem: A geographer scores two places at risk from earthquakes using the formula risk = hazard × vulnerability ÷ capacity to cope (all scores out of 10 except capacity, out of 4). Town A: hazard 8, vulnerability 8, capacity 2. Town C: hazard 5, vulnerability 9, capacity 1. (a) Calculate the risk score for Town A. (b) Explain why reducing vulnerability may be more realistic than reducing the hazard.
items.answer: (a) 32 (b) People cannot stop earthquakes happening, but they can improve buildings, reduce poverty and plan land use so fewer people are harmed.

items.stem: “The benefits of living in hazardous areas outweigh the risks.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: energy and tourism; risk management.
items.answer: Agree: Fertile volcanic soils (Java, Etna), geothermal energy (Iceland), tourism and jobs in big cities such as Tokyo and San Francisco. Large hazards are infrequent and monitoring reduces danger. Disagree: Major disasters can kill thousands and destroy livelihoods, e.g. Nepal 2015, Haiti 2010. Poorer people often live there because they have no choice, not because of benefits. Judgement: For most people most of the time benefits outweigh risks, especially where risk is managed well, but for the poorest the risks are much greater.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: A student writes: “People only live near volcanoes because they do not know about the danger.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many know the risks but stay for fertile land, jobs, geothermal energy and family ties, or because they cannot afford to move.

items.answer: Reasons: fertile volcanic soil gives good harvests; their land, home and community are there and they may not be able to afford land elsewhere. Reducing risk: monitoring and warning systems with evacuation plans; hazard maps showing lahar and pyroclastic flow paths; evacuation shelters and drills.

items.stem: Explain why the Tōhoku earthquake (magnitude 9.0) had a much higher economic cost than the Nepal earthquake (magnitude 7.8).
items.answer: Japan is a high-income country with expensive buildings, infrastructure, ports, factories and a nuclear power plant in the affected area; the tsunami destroyed property worth far more, so costs (estimated at over US$200 billion) were much higher.
items.markingKey: 1 mark value of property/infrastructure; 1 mark tsunami/nuclear damage [2]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why low-income countries often rely on international aid after a disaster.
items.answer: They lack money to pay for rescue and rebuilding; they have fewer trained rescue teams, helicopters and heavy equipment; hospitals and roads may be destroyed.

items.answer: They are estimates; counting is difficult in low-income or remote areas; some include people missing; different organisations give different totals.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reason; 1 mark development [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that a country’s level of development is the most important factor affecting the impact of an earthquake.
items.answer: Agree: Wealthier countries have building codes, warning systems and emergency services: Chile 2010 (8.8) about 525 deaths vs Haiti 2010 (7.0) over 100 000. Wealth allows faster rebuilding. Disagree: Physical factors matter: magnitude, depth, distance to cities and secondary hazards (the Tōhoku tsunami killed about 18 500 in a high-income country). Time of day and population density matter. Governance and preparation vary within the same income level. Judgement: Development is usually the most important factor in deaths, but physical factors can overwhelm even rich countries.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Explain why long-term responses are as important as immediate responses.
items.answer: Immediate responses save lives, but long-term responses (rebuilding with better codes, restoring jobs and services, improving warnings) reduce the impact of the next disaster and help the economy recover.
items.markingKey: 1 mark immediate saves lives; 1 mark long-term reduces future risk [2]

items.stem: Describe the differences between oceanic and continental crust.
items.answer: Oceanic: thinner (5-10 km), denser (basalt), younger, can be subducted. Continental: thicker (25-70 km), less dense (granite), older, is not subducted.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “hazard”?
options: Heat energy from rocks below the Earth’s surface, used to heat homes and generate electricity.
Moving people away from a dangerous area before or during a hazard.
A flexible pad or spring placed under a building to absorb earthquake shaking.
A natural event, such as an earthquake or eruption, that threatens people and property.

items.stem: Explain why earthquakes are much harder to predict than volcanic eruptions.
items.answer: Volcanoes give warning signs such as swelling, small earthquakes and gas emissions that can be monitored; stress building on a fault cannot be measured precisely, so scientists can only give probabilities.

items.stem: Tokyo has over 35 million people in its metropolitan area and lies in one of the most earthquake-prone regions on Earth. Explain two reasons why the city continues to grow despite the risk.
items.answer: It is Japan’s capital and economic centre with many jobs and services; Japan’s strict building codes, warning systems and drills make people feel the risk is managed; large earthquakes are infrequent.

items.stem: Explain why the earthquake in Haiti (2010) killed so many more people than the stronger earthquake in Chile (2010).
items.answer: Haiti is a low-income country: buildings in Port-au-Prince were poorly constructed and densely packed, building codes were not enforced, and emergency services were weak; Chile had strict building codes and experienced earthquake planning. Haiti’s epicentre was also very close to the capital and shallow.
items.markingKey: 1 mark buildings/codes; 1 mark emergency capacity; 1 mark location/depth [3]

items.stem: Compare two earthquakes. Chile 2010: magnitude 8.8  about 525 deaths  upper-middle income country. Nepal 2015: magnitude 7.8  about 9 000 deaths  low income country. (Death figures are estimates.) Describe the relationship between magnitude and deaths shown by these two examples.
items.answer: The stronger earthquake (Chile 2010) caused fewer deaths, so magnitude alone does not explain deaths.
items.markingKey: 1 mark relationship; 1 mark data [2]

items.stem: How far do you agree that international aid is the most important response to disasters in low-income countries? Use your own knowledge to support your answer. You may wish to consider: immediate aid; local responses.
items.answer: Agree: Aid provides money, rescue teams, medicine and shelter that local governments cannot supply, e.g. in Nepal 2015. Disagree: Local people and communities carry out most rescues in the first hours. Long-term reconstruction, governance and better building matter most for future disasters. Aid can be slow, poorly coordinated or create dependency (Haiti after 2010). Judgement: Aid is vital in the short term, but local capacity and long-term reconstruction decide how well a country recovers.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Explain how convection currents in the mantle are thought to move tectonic plates.
items.answer: Heat from the core makes mantle rock rise, spread beneath the plates and sink as it cools; this slow circular flow drags the plates along (helped by ridge push and slab pull).
items.markingKey: 1 mark heating/rising; 1 mark cooling/sinking; 1 mark drags plates [3]

items.stem: Scientists measure that the Nazca plate moving towards the South American plate move together at about 7 cm per year. (a) Name the type of plate boundary. (b) Explain what causes the plates to move.
items.answer: (a) Destructive (or collision) (b) Convection currents in the mantle, together with ridge push and slab pull.

items.stem: How far do you agree that the theory of plate tectonics explains where most of the world’s earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains are found? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
items.answer: Agree: Most earthquakes and volcanoes lie along plate boundaries such as the Ring of Fire; fold mountains such as the Himalayas and Andes form where plates converge. Disagree: Hotspots such as Hawaii form volcanoes in the middle of plates. Some earthquakes happen away from boundaries, along old faults or because of human activity such as mining. Judgement: Plate tectonics explains the great majority of these features, with hotspots and intraplate earthquakes as exceptions.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the immediate effects of a hazard, such as collapsed buildings and deaths caused directly by shaking or lava”.
items.answer: Primary effects
items.markingKey: Primary effects: the immediate effects of a hazard, such as collapsed buildings and deaths caused directly by shaking or lava. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “An earthquake of magnitude 8 is twice as powerful as one of magnitude 4.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. The scale is logarithmic: each whole number is about 32 times more energy, so magnitude 8 releases about a million times more energy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how an earthquake at sea can cause a tsunami.
items.answer: The sudden upward movement of the sea floor at a subduction zone displaces a huge volume of water, creating waves that travel across the ocean and grow taller in shallow water near the coast.
items.markingKey: 1 mark sea floor displaced; 1 mark waves build in shallow water [2]

items.stem: Case study: Chile 2010. On 27 February 2010 an earthquake of magnitude 8.8 struck off the coast of central Chile. It was caused by the Nazca plate subducting beneath the South American plate (destructive boundary). Deaths: about 525. Classify one of the effects you described as primary or secondary, and explain your choice.
items.answer: E.g. building collapse is primary because it was caused directly by shaking; landslides, tsunami, disease or loss of income are secondary because they followed from the shaking.
items.markingKey: 1 mark classification; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Study Source A, a newspaper report from Kathmandu, 26 April 2015 (adapted). “The nine-storey Dharahara tower, a symbol of the city, collapsed in seconds. Families slept in the open, afraid of aftershocks, while rescuers dug through the rubble of brick houses with their bare hands.” Suggest the purpose of Source A. Explain your answer.
items.answer: To report the disaster quickly to readers in Nepal and around the world.
items.markingKey: 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2]

items.stem: “Secondary effects of earthquakes are more serious than primary effects.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: long-term economic effects; Haiti 2010.
items.answer: Agree: The Tōhoku tsunami (2011) caused over 90% of deaths and the Fukushima nuclear accident. In Haiti (2010) a cholera outbreak later killed thousands; landslides cut off Nepali villages in 2015. Disagree: In many earthquakes, such as Nepal 2015 and Haiti 2010, most deaths came from buildings collapsing during the shaking. Primary effects destroy homes and infrastructure needed for recovery. Judgement: It depends on the event: for coastal subduction earthquakes secondary effects are often worse, for inland earthquakes primary effects usually dominate.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: What is meant by the term “risk”?
options: Using instruments such as seismometers, tiltmeters and gas sensors to watch for signs of a hazard.
How likely people are to be harmed by a hazard, depending on factors such as poverty and building quality.
A map showing areas at greatest risk from a hazard, used to plan land use and evacuation routes.
The chance of a hazard causing loss of life or damage, which increases with vulnerability.
items.answer: The chance of a hazard causing loss of life or damage, which increases with vulnerability.
items.markingKey: Risk: the chance of a hazard causing loss of life or damage, which increases with vulnerability. [1]

items.stem: Explain how education and preparation can reduce deaths from hazards.
items.answer: Drills teach people to “drop, cover and hold on” or evacuate to high ground after a tsunami warning; emergency kits and family plans help people survive until help arrives.
items.markingKey: 1 mark action; 1 mark how it saves lives [2]

items.stem: A geographer scores two places at risk from earthquakes using the formula risk = hazard × vulnerability ÷ capacity to cope (all scores out of 10 except capacity, out of 4). Village D: hazard 9, vulnerability 5, capacity 1. Town B: hazard 5, vulnerability 9, capacity 4. (a) Calculate the risk score for Village D. (b) State which place is at greater risk. (c) Suggest two ways to increase a place’s capacity to cope.
items.answer: (a) 45 (b) Village D (45 compared with 11.2) (c) Train emergency services, build earthquake-resistant hospitals, set up warning systems, hold drills, store emergency supplies.

items.stem: A geographer scores two places at risk from earthquakes using the formula risk = hazard × vulnerability ÷ capacity to cope (all scores out of 10 except capacity, out of 4). Town B: hazard 8, vulnerability 9, capacity 1. Town A: hazard 7, vulnerability 6, capacity 3. (a) Calculate the risk score for Town A. (b) Explain why reducing vulnerability may be more realistic than reducing the hazard.
items.answer: (a) 14 (b) People cannot stop earthquakes happening, but they can improve buildings, reduce poverty and plan land use so fewer people are harmed.
items.markingKey: (a) 7 × 6 ÷ 3 = 14 [1] (b) 1 mark hazard cannot be controlled; 1 mark vulnerability can be reduced [2]

items.stem: How far do you agree that prediction is the most effective way of reducing the impact of tectonic hazards? Use your own knowledge to support your answer. You may wish to consider: building design; warning systems.
items.answer: Agree: Monitoring allowed the Pinatubo evacuation (1991); tsunami warnings give time to reach high ground. Disagree: Earthquakes cannot be predicted precisely, so protection (building design) saves more lives. Planning – hazard maps, drills, land-use rules – reduces vulnerability. Warnings only help if people receive them and know what to do. Judgement: Prediction is vital for volcanoes and tsunamis, but protection and planning matter more for earthquakes.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “International aid always reaches the people who need it most quickly.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Damaged roads, landslides, poor coordination and corruption can delay aid, as in rural Nepal in 2015.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Strict building codes help explain why Chile’s magnitude 8.8 earthquake in 2010 killed far fewer people than Haiti’s magnitude 7.0 earthquake.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Chile’s buildings were designed to withstand shaking; Haiti’s were not.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Compare two earthquakes. Christchurch 2011: magnitude 6.2  about 185 deaths  high income country. Nepal 2015: magnitude 7.8  about 9 000 deaths  low income country. (Death figures are estimates.) Describe the relationship between magnitude and deaths shown by these two examples.
items.answer: The stronger earthquake also caused more deaths here, but development and secondary effects also matter.
items.markingKey: 1 mark relationship; 1 mark data [2]

items.stem: “A country’s level of development is the most important factor affecting the impact of an earthquake.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: Haiti and Chile 2010; Nepal 2015.
items.answer: Agree: Wealthier countries have building codes, warning systems and emergency services: Chile 2010 (8.8) about 525 deaths vs Haiti 2010 (7.0) over 100 000. Wealth allows faster rebuilding. Disagree: Physical factors matter: magnitude, depth, distance to cities and secondary hazards (the Tōhoku tsunami killed about 18 500 in a high-income country). Time of day and population density matter. Governance and preparation vary within the same income level. Judgement: Development is usually the most important factor in deaths, but physical factors can overwhelm even rich countries.
